knowledge_units.context_summary: The study demonstrates that the enzyme SERCA regulates paramyxovirus replication and that its inhibitor, Thapsigargin, reduces viral entry and protein localization. While Newcastle disease virus (NDV) acquired resistance to Thapsigargin after long-term passage, Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) did not.

knowledge_units.context_summary: Vertebrate P-type calcium ATPases, including SERCA, PMCA, and SPCA, regulate intracellular calcium homeostasis in specific organelles. SERCA is encoded by three genes that undergo alternative splicing to produce ten isoforms with varying expression patterns. Thapsigargin, a non-competitive SERCA inhibitor, was identified from a kinase inhibitor library as a compound that blocks paramyxovirus replication.

transports Ca2+ from cytosol to intracellular compartments

knowledge_units.context_summary: Thapsigargin, a SERCA inhibitor, was tested for cytotoxicity and antiviral efficacy against paramyxoviruses and DNA viruses. The study found that Thapsigargin inhibits paramyxovirus replication without direct virucidal effects, and that SERCA2 overexpression rescues this inhibition. PPRV infection was shown to induce SERCA2 expression in Vero cells.

relationships.target: inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin on virus replication

knowledge_units.context_summary: Thapsigargin treatment blocks virus-induced SERCA2 expression and specifically inhibits paramyxovirus entry and protein localization. Time-of-addition assays indicate that the inhibitor affects pre-budding stages of the viral life cycle for both NDV and PPRV. Immunofluorescence reveals that SERCA inhibition causes defective subcellular localization of viral proteins, trapping them in cytoplasmic foci rather than at the cell surface.

relationships.target: virus attachment, RNA synthesis, and budding

attributes.purpose: ascertain viral life cycle stages impaired by Thapsigargin

relationships.target: multiple pre-budding steps of paramyxovirus replication

knowledge_units.context_summary: Thapsigargin treatment causes defective subcellular localization of viral proteins in approximately 70% of infected cells, compared to 10-30% in controls. Sequential passage of Newcastle disease virus (NDV) in the presence of Thapsigargin leads to partial resistance, whereas Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) does not develop resistance. The study suggests that host-targeting agents like SERCA inhibitors impose a higher genetic barrier to resistance than direct viral targets.

attributes.function: required for proper localization of viral proteins from cytoplasm to cell surface

attributes.advantage: higher genetic barrier to resistance due to low host genetic variability

While NDV acquired partial resistance to Thapsigargin after long-term passage, PPRV did not, suggesting a unique mechanism of host-factor dependency bypass in NDV.
